A Variational Inequality Perspective on Generative Adversarial Nets

Gauthier Gidel Affiliation: Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms (MILA) & DIRO Université de Montréal    Hugo Berard Affiliation: Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms (MILA) & DIRO Université de Montréal Affiliation: Facebook Artificial Intelligence Research    Pascal Vincent Affiliation: Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms (MILA) & DIRO Université de Montréal Affiliation: Facebook Artificial Intelligence Research Affiliation: CIFAR fellow    Simon Lacoste-Julien Correspondence to: firstname.name@umontreal.ca Affiliation: Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms (MILA) & DIRO Université de Montréal Affiliation: CIFAR fellow
Abstract

Stability has been a recurrent issue in training generative adversarial networks (GANs). One common way to tackle this issue has been to propose new formulations of the GAN objective. Yet, surprisingly few studies have looked at optimization methods specifically designed for this adversarial training. In this work, we review the “variational inequality” framework which contains most formulations of the GAN objective introduced so far. Taping into the mathematical programming literature, we counter some common misconceptions about the difficulties of saddle point optimization and propose to extend standard methods designed for variational inequalities to GANs training, such as a stochastic version of the extragradient method, and empirically investigate their behavior on GANs.

Keywords:
Machine Learning, ICML
††affiliationnotice: Equal contribution

1 Introduction

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) (Goodfellow et al., 2014) form an approach to generative modeling known for producing appealing samples such as for image generation. Nevertheless, GANs are also known to be hard to train, often displaying an unstable behavior. Much recent research has been devoted to try to stabilize the training of GANs. One common way to tackle this issue has been to propose new formulations of the GAN objective (Nowozin et al., 2016; Arjovsky et al., 2017).

In this work, we opt instead to leverage standard techniques coming from the mathematical programming literature. In particular, we point out that most GAN settings proposed so far can be cast as a variational inequality problem (Harker and Pang, 1990), which is also the general framework within which saddle point optimization algorithms were developed (Korpelevich, 1976). Consequently, we propose to tap into this literature and apply its standard methods to train GANs. We will also show that some of the issues of GAN training noticed so far can be explained with standard variational inequality optimization results. Moreover, we introduce a novel setting able to handle the non-boundedness of the model parameters and the non-convexity of the cost functions (by only assuming local convexity), which are non-standard assumptions in the variational inequality literature.

Contributions. We introduce for the first time an analysis of GANs objectives within the framework of variational inequality, well-known in optimization. We bring from the related literature standard methods and results to solve variational inequalities, namely averaging the iterates as well as the extragradient method. We extend their analysis to the specificity of GANs training, namely stochasticity, non-boundedness and local convexity. Finally, we provide experimental evidence on the ability of these methods to stabilize GANs training.

This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the background on GANs and on optimization. Section 3 explains how to cast the optimization problem of GANs as a variational inequality and reviews the framework. Section 4 introduces the standard methods to optimize variational inequalities and Section 5 presents the experimental results.

2 Background

GANs formulations.

We start with the generative adversarial net formulation understood as divergence minimization (Liu et al., 2017), before presenting alternative viewpoints in terms of game theory (Arora et al., 2017) later in this section. We want to generate samples from a distribution qθq_{\theta} that matches best the true distribution pp of the data. For this purpose, the GAN approach implicitly defines a divergence Div(p||qθ)\Div(p||q_{\theta}) via a maximization problem that quantifies the quality of qθq_{\theta}, and the goal is to find qθq_{\theta} that minimizes this divergence. In this paper, we focus on finite dimensional optimization for simplicity and thus consider a parametric formulation of the divergence. Most of the parametric divergences encountered in the GAN literature can be formulated as so-called parametric adversarial divergences (Huang et al., 2017):

Div(p||qθ)=defsupϕ∈Φ𝔼(𝒙,𝒙′)∼p⊗qθ[Δ(fϕ(𝒙),fϕ(𝒙′))],\Div(p||q_{\theta})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}{\mathbb{E}}_{({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime})\sim p\otimes{q_{\theta}}}[\Delta(f_{\phi}({\bm{x}}),f_{\phi}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}))]\,, (1)

where the functions of the class {fϕ;ϕ∈Φ}\{f_{\phi}\;;\;\phi\in\Phi\} are called the discriminators, and are usually neural nets. The constraints on Φ\Phi and the function Δ\Delta determine properties of the resulting divergence, studied among others by Liu et al. (2017); Arora et al. (2017); Huang et al. (2017). For example, by choosing Δ⁡(fϕ​(𝒙),fϕ​(𝒙′))=fϕ​(𝒙)−fϕ​(𝒙′)\Delta(f_{\phi}({\bm{x}}),f_{\phi}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}))=f_{\phi}({\bm{x}})-f_{\phi}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}) and constraining fϕf_{\phi} to belong to the class of 1-Lipschitz functions, we get the (parametric) Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) objective proposed by Arjovsky et al. (2017):

minθ∈Θ⁡maxϕ∈Φ,‖fϕ‖L≤1​𝔼𝒙∼p​[fϕ​(𝒙)]−𝔼𝒙′∼qθ​[fϕ​(𝒙′)].\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{\phi\in\Phi,||f_{\phi}||_{L}\leq 1}{\mathbb{E}}_{{\bm{x}}\sim p}[f_{\phi}({\bm{x}})]-{\mathbb{E}}_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\sim q_{\theta}}[f_{\phi}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})]. (2)

To sum up, the GAN objective (1) can be simply written as,

minθ∈Θ⁡maxϕ∈Φ​ℒ¯​(θ,ϕ).\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{\phi\in\Phi}\bar{\mathcal{L}}(\theta,\phi)\,. (SP)

One interpretation of the saddle point problem (SP) is that the two agents are playing a game where the generator tries to minimize a cost function that the discriminator simultaneously tries to maximize. The goal of the learning procedure is to find a pair achieving such minimax (SP). It is called a saddle point when the minimization and the maximization can be switched in (SP). This is the case e.g. when ℒ¯\bar{\mathcal{L}} is convex-concave (definition in App. A) and Θ\Theta, Φ\Phi are bounded; such a point is also called a Nash equilibrium (Nash et al., 1950).

Equilibrium.

The minimax formulation is theoretically convenient because a large literature on games studies this problem and provides guaranties on the existence of equilibria. Nevertheless, practical considerations lead the GAN literature to consider a different objective for each player. In that case, the two-players game problem (Von Neumann and Morgenstern, 1944) is to find (θ∗,ϕ∗)∈Θ×Φ(\theta^{*},\phi^{*})\in\Theta\times\Phi so that

{θ∗∈𝐚𝐫𝐠​𝐦𝐢𝐧θ∈Θ⁡ℒ(θ)​(θ,ϕ∗)ϕ∗∈𝐚𝐫𝐠​𝐦𝐢𝐧ϕ∈Φ⁡ℒ(ϕ)​(θ∗,ϕ).\left\{\begin{aligned} &\theta^{*}\in\argmin_{\theta\in\Theta}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\theta)}(\theta,\phi^{*})\\ &\phi^{*}\in\argmin_{\phi\in\Phi}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\phi)}(\theta^{*},\phi)\,.\\[-5.69054pt] \end{aligned}\right. (3)

Particularly, when ℒ(θ)=−ℒ(ϕ){\mathcal{L}}^{(\theta)}=-{\mathcal{L}}^{(\phi)} the game is called a zero-sum game and the optimization problem can be formulated as a saddle point problem (SP). Even if the minimax formulation of the GANs is the one used for most of the theoretical analysis, in practice Goodfellow et al. (2014) recommend to use a formulation called non-saturating GAN which is not a zero-sum game (as noted by Mescheder et al. (2017)):

ℒ(θ)​(θ,ϕ)=def−𝔼𝒙′∼qθ​log⁡fϕ​(𝒙′)\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}^{(\theta)}(\theta,\phi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}-\underset{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\sim q_{\theta}}{\mathbb{E}}\log f_{\phi}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})
ℒ(ϕ)​(θ,ϕ)=def−𝔼𝒙∼p​log⁡fϕ​(𝒙)−𝔼𝒙′∼qθ​log⁡(1−fϕ​(𝒙′)).\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}^{(\phi)}(\theta,\phi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}-\!\!\underset{{\bm{x}}\sim p}{\mathbb{E}}\!\!\log f_{\phi}({\bm{x}})-\!\!\underset{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\sim q_{\theta}}{\mathbb{E}}\!\!\log(1-f_{\phi}({\bm{x}}^{\prime}))\,.

One important point to notice is that the two optimization problems in (3) are coupled and have to be considered jointly from an optimization point of view. On the other hand, standard GANs are non-convex (i.e. each cost function is non-convex), and thus such equilibria may not exist, bringing optimization issues. In particular, when no equilibrium exists, following the gradient may be unstable and lead to iterates with a constantly growing norm. Even if an equilibrium point does exist, a bad initialization may lead to the same unwanted behavior.

Proving the existence of an equilibrium in GANs is outside the scope of this work. Instead in the following we focus on ways to optimize these games assuming that an equilibrium exists. As is often standard in non-convex optimization, we will also focus on finding points satisfying the necessary stationary conditions (though which are not automatically sufficient unless there is some local convexity). As we mentioned previously, one of the emerging difficulty and difference between the standard minimization and the optimization of such games is that the optimization of the two different cost functions of (3) has to be done jointly in θ\theta and ϕ\phi. Fortunately, the optimization literature has studied for a long time what is called variational inequality problems which generalizes the stationary conditions for two player games problems. Before introducing this setting, as a teaser, we present the behavior of standard algorithms to variational inequalities on a simple GAN optimization problem.

The bilinear WGAN.

We consider a toy example where the discriminator and the generator are linear: Dϕ​(𝒙)=fϕ​(𝒙)=ϕT​𝒙D_{\phi}({\bm{x}})=f_{\phi}({\bm{x}})=\phi^{T}{\bm{x}} and Gθ​(𝒛)=θ​𝒛G_{\theta}({\bm{z}})=\theta{\bm{z}} (implicitly defining qθq_{\theta}). By replacing these expressions in the WGAN objective, we get the following bilinear objective:

minθ∈Θ⁡maxϕ∈Φ,‖ϕ‖≤1​ϕT​𝔼​[𝑿]−ϕT​θ​𝔼​[𝒁].\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{\phi\in\Phi,||\phi||\leq 1}\phi^{T}{\mathbb{E}}[{\bm{X}}]-\phi^{T}\theta{\mathbb{E}}[{\bm{Z}}]\,. (4)

A similar task was presented in (Nagarajan and Kolter, 2017) where they consider a quadratic discriminator instead of a linear one, and show that gradient descent is not necessarily asymptotically stable. The bilinear objective has been extensively used (Goodfellow, 2016; Mescheder, 2018; Yadav et al., 2018) to highlight the difficulties of gradient descent for saddle point optimization. Yet, this phenomenon has been extensively studied in the mathematical programming literature and simple fixes were proposed such as averaging the iterates or adding an extrapolation step (extragradient method), as we will describe in Section 4, with provable convergence guarantees even for the bilinear problem. We plot the behavior of these algorithms in Figure 1 for the simple case of the 2D bilinear objective of (4). Note that contrary to current common beliefs in machine learning on saddle point optimization, some of the proposed gradient based methods do converge to the equilibrium.

3 GANs as a Variational inequality

We first consider the local necessary conditions that characterize the solution of the smooth two-players game (3), defining stationary points, which will motivate the definition of a variational inequality. In the unconstrained setting, a stationary point is a couple (θ∗,ϕ∗)(\theta^{*},\phi^{*}) with zero gradient:

‖∇θℒ(θ)​(θ∗,ϕ∗)‖=‖∇ϕℒ(ϕ)​(θ∗,ϕ∗)‖=0.\|\nabla_{\theta}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\theta)}(\theta^{*},\phi^{*})\|=\|\nabla_{\phi}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\phi)}(\theta^{*},\phi^{*})\|=0\,. (5)

In the constrained optimization setting (which can occur when the parameters are clipped (Arjovsky et al., 2017)) a stationary point (θ∗,ϕ∗)(\theta^{*},\phi^{*}) is such that the directional derivative of each cost function is non-negative in any feasible direction (and thus there is no feasible descent direction):

{∇θℒ(θ)​(θ∗,ϕ∗)⊤​(θ−θ∗)≥0,∇ϕℒ(ϕ)​(θ∗,ϕ∗)⊤​(ϕ−ϕ∗)≥0∀(θ,ϕ)∈Θ×Φ.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\!\nabla_{\theta}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\theta)}(\theta^{*},\phi^{*})^{\top}\!(\theta-\theta^{*})\geq 0\,,\\ &\!\nabla_{\phi}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\phi)}(\theta^{*},\phi^{*})^{\top}\!(\phi-\phi^{*})\geq 0\end{aligned}\right.\;\;\forall\,(\theta,\phi)\in\Theta\times\Phi. (6)

Defining 𝒙=def(θ,ϕ),𝒙∗=def(θ∗,ϕ∗),𝒳=defΘ×Φ{\bm{x}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}(\theta,\phi),\,{\bm{x}}^{*}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}(\theta^{*},\phi^{*}),\,{\mathcal{X}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\Theta\times\Phi and,

F⁡(𝒙)=def(∇θℒ(θ)​(θ,ϕ)∇ϕℒ(ϕ)​(θ,ϕ)),F({\bm{x}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\begin{pmatrix}\nabla_{\theta}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\theta)}(\theta,\phi)\\ \nabla_{\phi}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\phi)}(\theta,\phi)\end{pmatrix}\,, (7)

the stationary conditions can be compactly formulated as:

F​(𝒙∗)⊤​(𝒙−𝒙∗)≥0,∀𝒙∈𝒳.F({\bm{x}}^{*})^{\top}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}^{*})\geq 0\,,\;\;\forall{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}\,. (8)

Finding such a 𝒙∗{\bm{x}}^{*} is called a variational inequality problem.

3.1 Variational inequalities for convex cost functions

Let 𝒳⊂ℝd{\mathcal{X}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and let F:𝒳→ℝdF\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}{\mathcal{X}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{d} be a continuous mapping. The variational inequality problem (Harker and Pang, 1990) is the following problem:

find​𝒙∗∈𝒳:F​(𝒙∗)⊤​(𝒙−𝒙∗)≥0,∀𝒙∈𝒳.\text{find}\;{\bm{x}}^{*}\in{\mathcal{X}}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\;F({\bm{x}}^{*})^{\top}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}^{*})\geq 0\,,\;\;\forall{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}\,. (VIP)

We will call optimal set the set 𝒳∗{\mathcal{X}}^{*} of 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} verifying (VIP). A standard assumption on FF is its monotonicity:

(F⁡(𝒙)−F⁡(𝒚))⊤​(𝒙−𝒚)≥0∀𝒙,𝒚∈𝒳.(F({\bm{x}})-F({\bm{y}}))^{\top}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}})\geq 0\quad\forall\,{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{X}}\,. (9)

If F​(𝒙)=∇f​(𝒙)F({\bm{x}})=\nabla f({\bm{x}}), it is equivalent to ff being convex. If FF can be written as (7), it implies that the cost functions are convex.11 1 The convexity of the cost functions in (3) is a necessary condition (but not sufficient) for the operator to be monotone. When we are in the context of saddle point optimization (SP), the convexity of the cost functions is a sufficient condition. When the operator FF is monotone, we have that F​(𝒙∗)⊤​(𝒙−𝒙∗)≤F​(𝒙)⊤​(𝒙−𝒙∗),∀𝒙,𝒙∗F({\bm{x}}^{*})^{\top}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}^{*})\leq F({\bm{x}})^{\top}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}^{*})\,,\;\forall{\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{*}. Hence, in this case (VIP) implies a stronger formulation sometimes called Minty variational inequality (Crespi et al., 2005):

find​𝒙∗∈𝒳:F​(𝒙)⊤​(𝒙−𝒙∗)≥0,∀𝒙∈𝒳.\text{find}\;{\bm{x}}^{*}\in{\mathcal{X}}\;\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\;F({\bm{x}})^{\top}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}^{*})\geq 0\,,\;\;\forall{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}\,. (MVI)

This formulation is stronger in the sense that if (MVI) holds for some 𝒙∗∈𝒳{\bm{x}}^{*}\in{\mathcal{X}}, then (VIP) holds too. This second formulation has two advantages: first it gives us a global criterion for a solution which can be used even in the non-monotone setting22 2 In the context of GANs, the cost functions being non-convex yields a non-monotone operator. and secondly, we can derive from this formulation a merit function that we can use in our analysis. Roughly, a merit function is a quantitative convergence measure.

More formally, a function g:𝒳→ℝg\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}{\mathcal{X}}\to{\mathbb{R}}\, is called a merit function if gg is a non-negative function such that g⁡(𝒙)=0⇔𝒙∈𝒳∗g({\bm{x}})=0\Leftrightarrow{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}^{*} (Larsson and Patriksson, 1994). A natural way to derive a merit function from (MVI) would be to use g⁡(𝒙∗)=sup𝒙∈XF​(𝒙)⊤​(𝒙∗−𝒙)g({\bm{x}}^{*})=\sup_{{\bm{x}}\in X}F({\bm{x}})^{\top}({\bm{x}}^{*}-{\bm{x}}) which is 0 if and only if (MVI) hold for 𝒙∗{\bm{x}}^{*}. But to deal with a potentially unbounded constraint set (leading to a potentially infinite valued function outside of the optimal set), we will use the restricted merit function introduced by Nesterov (2007):

ErrR(VI)⁡(𝒙t)=defmax𝒙∈𝒳,‖𝒙−𝒙0‖≤R⁡F​(𝒙)⊤​(𝒙t−𝒙).\Err_{R}^{(\text{VI})}({\bm{x}}_{t})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\max_{{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}},\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}_{0}\|\leq R}F({\bm{x}})^{\top}({\bm{x}}_{t}-{\bm{x}})\,. (10)

This function acts as merit function for (VIP) on the interior of the open ball of radius RR around 𝒙0{\bm{x}}_{0}, as shown in Lemma 1 of Nesterov (2007). That is, let 𝒳R:=𝒳∩{𝒙:∥𝒙−𝒙0∥<R}{\mathcal{X}}_{R}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}={\mathcal{X}}\cap\{{\bm{x}}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}{\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}_{0}\|<R}\}. Then for any point 𝒙^∈𝒳R\hat{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}_{R}, we have:

ErrR(VI)⁡(𝒙^)=0⇔𝒙^∈𝒳∗∩𝒳R.\Err_{R}^{(\text{VI})}(\hat{\bm{x}})=0\Leftrightarrow\hat{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}^{*}\cap{\mathcal{X}}_{R}. (11)

The reference point 𝒙0{\bm{x}}_{0} is arbitrary, but in practice it is usually the initialization point of the algorithm. RR has to be big enough to ensure that 𝒳R{\mathcal{X}}_{R} contains a solution. ErrR\Err_{R} basically measures how much (MVI) is violated on the restriction 𝒳R{\mathcal{X}}_{R}.

Such merit function is standard in the variational inequality literature. Similar ones are used in (Nemirovski, 2004; Juditsky et al., 2011). When the objective is a saddle point problem (SP) where ℒ¯\bar{\mathcal{L}} is convex-concave (see definition in App. A), we can use another merit function on 𝒳R{\mathcal{X}}_{R} that is more interpretable and more directly related to the cost function of the minimax formulation:

ErrR(SP)⁡(θt,ϕt)=defmaxϕ∈Φ,θ∈Θ‖(θ,ϕ)−(θ0,ϕ0)‖≤R⁡ℒ¯​(θt,ϕ)−ℒ¯​(θ,ϕt).\Err_{R}^{(\text{SP})}(\theta_{t},\phi_{t})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\phi\in\Phi,\theta\in\Theta\\ \|(\theta,\phi)-(\theta_{0},\phi_{0})\|\leq R\end{subarray}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\bar{\mathcal{L}}(\theta_{t},\phi)-\bar{\mathcal{L}}(\theta,\phi_{t})\,. (12)

In particular, if the equilibrium (θ∗,ϕ∗)∈𝒳∗∩𝒳R(\theta^{*},\phi^{*})\in{\mathcal{X}}^{*}\cap{\mathcal{X}}_{R} and we have that ℒ¯​(⋅,ϕ∗)\bar{\mathcal{L}}(\cdot,\phi^{*}) and −ℒ¯​(θ∗,⋅)-\bar{\mathcal{L}}(\theta^{*},\cdot) are μ\mu-strongly convex (see App. A), then the merit function for saddle points upper bounds the distance for (θ,ϕ)∈𝒳R(\theta,\phi)\in{\mathcal{X}}_{R} to the equilibrium as:

ErrR(SP)⁡(θ,ϕ)≥μ2​(‖θ−θ∗‖22+‖ϕ−ϕ∗‖22).\Err_{R}^{(\text{SP})}(\theta,\phi)\geq\frac{\mu}{2}(\|\theta-\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\phi-\phi^{*}\|_{2}^{2})\,. (13)

We will provide our convergence results with the merit functions (10) and (12), depending on the setup:

ErrR(𝒙)=def{ErrR(SP)⁡(𝒙)if F is a SP operator (7)ErrR(VI)⁡(𝒙)otherwise.\Err_{R}({\bm{x}})\!\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\!\left\{\begin{aligned} \Err_{R}^{(\text{SP})}({\bm{x}})\;\;&\text{if $F$ is a SP operator\penalty\ \eqref{eq:SP_operator}}\\ \Err_{R}^{(\text{VI})}({\bm{x}})\;\;&\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right. (14)

3.2 On the importance of the merit function

In this section, we illustrate the fact that one has to be careful when extending results and properties from the minimization setting to the minimax setting (and consequently to the variational inequality setting). Another candidate as a merit function for saddle point optimization would be to naturally extend the suboptimality f⁡(𝒙)−f⁡(𝒙∗)f({\bm{x}})-f({\bm{x}}^{*}) used in standard minimization (i.e. find 𝒙∗{\bm{x}}^{*} the minimizer of ff) to the gap P⁡(θ,ϕ)=ℒ¯​(θ,ϕ∗)−ℒ¯​(θ∗,ϕ)P(\theta,\phi)=\bar{\mathcal{L}}(\theta,\phi^{*})-\bar{\mathcal{L}}(\theta^{*},\phi). In a previous analysis of a modification of the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) method for GANs, Yadav et al. (2018) gave their convergence rate on PP that they called the “primal-dual“ gap. Unfortunately, if we do not assume that the function ℒ¯\bar{\mathcal{L}} is strongly convex-concave (a stronger assumption defined in App. A and which fails for bilinear objective e.g.), PP may not be a merit function. It can be 0 for a non optimal point, see for instance the discussion on the differences between (12) and PP in (Gidel et al., 2017, Section 3). In particular, for the simple 2D bilinear example ℒ¯​(θ,ϕ)=θ⋅ϕ\bar{\mathcal{L}}(\theta,\phi)=\theta\cdot\phi, we have that θ∗=ϕ∗=0\theta^{*}=\phi^{*}=0 and thus P⁡(θ,ϕ)=0​∀θ,ϕP(\theta,\phi)=0\,\;\;\forall\theta,\phi\,.

3.3 Variational inequalities for non-convex cost functions

When the cost functions defined in (3) are non-convex, the operator FF is no longer monotone. Nevertheless, (VIP) and (MVI) still hold with the inconvenience that there may exist no solution to both of the global variational inequality problems. A less restrictive way to consider variational inequalities in the non-monotone setting is to use a local version of (VIP) and (MVI). If the cost functions are locally convex around the optimal couple (θ∗,ϕ∗)(\theta^{*},\phi^{*}) and if our iterates eventually fall and stay into that neighborhood, then we can consider our restricted merit function ErrR⁡(⋅)\Err_{R}(\cdot) with a well suited constant RR and apply our results for monotone operators.

4 Optimization of Variational Inequalities

As mentioned in Section 3, both saddle point optimization and game optimization can be cast as variational inequality problems. In this section, we present methods to solve (VIP).

4.1 Standard batch methods

The two standard methods studied in the (VIP) literature are the gradient method (Bruck, 1977) and the extragradient method (Korpelevich, 1976). The iterates of the gradient method are known to converge linearly when the operator is strongly monotone33 3 The strong monotonicity of an operator is a generalization of the strong convexity of a cost function. See Appendix A. (Chen and Rockafellar, 1997), but oscillates for a bilinear operator as showed in Fig. 1. On the other hand, the uniform average of the iterates of the gradient method converges for any monotone operator with a O⁡(1/t)O(1/\sqrt{t}) rate (Nedić and Ozdaglar, 2009). More generally, we will consider later a weighted averaging scheme,44 4 This weighted averaging scheme has been proposed for the first time for (batch) variational inequalities by Bruck (1977) and has been studied more recently in the context of SGD for convex minimization by Lacoste-Julien et al. (2012) (and references therein). with weights ρt≥0\rho_{t}\geq 0, defined as:

𝒙¯T=def∑t=0T−1ρt​𝒙tST,ST=def∑t=0T−1ρt.\bar{\bm{x}}_{T}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\frac{\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\rho_{t}{\bm{x}}_{t}}{S_{T}}\,,\quad S_{T}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\rho_{t}\,. (15)

Finally, the extragradient method does not require any averaging to converge for monotone operators, and can even converge at the faster O⁡(1/t)O(1/t) rate (Nesterov, 2007). The idea of this method is to compute a lookahead step (see extrapolation step in Alg. 2 and Alg. 3) in order to compute a more stable direction to follow. As we have seen in Fig. 1 (see also Fig. 3), oscillations for the gradient method may result from the game between the generator and the discriminator. The extragradient method takes advantage of the regularity of FF to prevent such oscillations.

4.2 Stochastic extensions

We present extensions of these standard methods in the context of a stochastic operator, i.e. F⁡(𝒙):=𝔼ξ∼P​[F⁡(𝒙,ξ)]F({\bm{x}})\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}={\mathbb{E}}_{\xi\sim P}[F({\bm{x}},\xi)]. We assume that this expectation cannot be computed and that we can only sample ξ∼P\xi\sim P and compute F⁡(𝒙,ξ)F({\bm{x}},\xi). This is motivated from the GAN formulation where we only have access to a finite sample estimate of the expectation, and the gradients are usually computed on mini-batches. For GAN, ξ\xi is thus a mini-batch of points coming from the true data distribution pp and the generator distribution qθq_{\theta}. In the following, we focus on stochastic algorithms designed to solve (VIP). For GANs, these algorithms will use stochastic approximations of the gradients of the respective cost functions (7) of the discriminator and the generator. In order to cover the case of parameter clipping (Arjovsky et al., 2017), we will provide a projected version of the algorithms, where P𝒳​(𝒚)P_{\mathcal{X}}({\bm{y}}) denotes the projection onto 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} (see App. A). The main property we use is that the projection onto a convex set is a non-expansive mapping. Note that when 𝒳=ℝd{\mathcal{X}}={\mathbb{R}}^{d}, the projection is the identity mapping (unconstrained setting). For our analysis, we require that the variance of the stochastic operator is uniformly bounded by σ2\sigma^{2}:

Assumption 1.

𝔼ξ​[‖F⁡(𝒙)−F⁡(𝒙,ξ)‖2]≤σ2,∀𝒙∈𝒳.{\mathbb{E}}_{\xi}[\|F({\bm{x}})-F({\bm{x}},\xi)\|^{2}]\leq\sigma^{2}\,,\;\;\forall{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}\,.

For the analysis of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), we need the additional stronger assumption that the expected value of the squared norm of the stochastic operator is uniformly bounded by M2M^{2}:

Assumption 2.

𝔼ξ​[‖F⁡(𝒙,ξ)‖2]≤M2,∀𝒙∈X.{\mathbb{E}}_{\xi}[\|F({\bm{x}},\xi)\|^{2}]\leq M^{2}\,,\quad\forall{\bm{x}}\in X\,.

Assumption 1 is pretty standard in stochastic variational analysis. Assumption 2 is standard in stochastic convex optimization, but is quite strong. It is not verified for a simple unconstrained bilinear objective. This assumption only seems reasonable for bounded constraint sets, but it can be weakened to 𝔼ξ​[‖F⁡(𝒙t,ξ)‖2]≤M2{\mathbb{E}}_{\xi}[\|F({\bm{x}}_{t},\xi)\|^{2}]\leq M^{2} for the 𝒙t{\bm{x}}_{t} iterates computed by an algorithm. Note that in practice we have σ≪M\sigma\ll M. In the following, we present three algorithms: the first one is the stochastic extension of the gradient method for solving (VIP); the other two are stochastic extensions of the extragradient method.

Stochastic gradient method.

The gradient method to solve (VIP) is also known as the forward-backward algorithm. It has been studied with additive noise by Rosasco et al. (2014) in the general context of monotone inclusion and by Nemirovski et al. (2009) in the context of stochastic saddle point optimization. We have not found a proof of convergence rate for the stochastic variational inequality case in the literature, and thus we present it here. Note that Alg. 1 is a stochastic extension of Nemirovski et al. (2009)’s work.

Theorem 1.

Let FF be a stochastic monotone operator, let 𝐱∗{\bm{x}}^{*} be a solution of (VIP) and let R>‖𝐱0−𝐱∗‖R>\|{\bm{x}}_{0}-{\bm{x}}^{*}\|. Under Assumption 2 and 1, AvgSGD (Alg. 1) with constant step size γ\gamma has the following convergence rate for all T≥1T\geq 1,

𝔼⁡[ErrR⁡(𝒙¯T)]≤R22​γ​T+γ​M2+σ22,{\mathbb{E}}[\Err_{R}(\bar{\bm{x}}_{T})]\leq\frac{R^{2}}{2\gamma T}+\gamma\frac{M^{2}+\sigma^{2}}{2}\,, (16)

where 𝐱¯T:=1T​∑t=0T−1𝐱t\bar{\bm{x}}_{T}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}{\bm{x}}_{t} and ErrR\Err_{R} is defined in (14). Then γ=RT⁡(M2+σ2)\gamma=\frac{R}{\sqrt{T(M^{2}+\sigma^{2})}} gives, 𝔼⁡[ErrR⁡(𝐱¯T)]≤R​M2+σ2T.{\mathbb{E}}[\Err_{R}(\bar{\bm{x}}_{T})]\leq\frac{R\sqrt{M^{2}+\sigma^{2}}}{\sqrt{T}}\,.

The constant term γ⁡(M2+σ2)/2\gamma(M^{2}+\sigma^{2})/2 of (16) the right hand side is called the variance term. These kinds of bounds are standard in stochastic optimization. Note that a similar rate with an extra log factor can be obtained with γt=γt\gamma_{t}=\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{t}} and is provided in App. B. If we want to compare this variance term with the one of the SGD with prediction method (Yadav et al., 2018), we need to have the same convergence certificate. Fortunately, we can notice that their proof can be adapted to our convergence criterion (Using Lemma 2 in App. B) making appear an extra σ2/2\sigma^{2}/2 in their variance term. The latter can be summarized with our notation as (M2​(1+L)+σ2)/2(M^{2}(1+L)+\sigma^{2})/2 where the LL is the Lipschitz constant of the operator FF. Since M≫σM\gg\sigma, their variance term is then 1+L1+L time larger than the one provided by the AvgSGD method. In the following we will call this method (PreSGD).

Stochastic extragradient method.

The extragradient method takes advantage of the regularity of FF to prevent the oscillations due to the game between the discriminator and the generator. Consequently, it has a smaller variance term than (16). We present an extension of Juditsky et al. (2011)’s work adapted to a general convex set 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} (allowing the unconstrained case).

Theorem 2.

Let FF be a stochastic monotone operator, let 𝐱∗{\bm{x}}^{*} be a solution of (VIP) and let R>‖𝐱0−𝐱∗‖R>\|{\bm{x}}_{0}-{\bm{x}}^{*}\|. Under Assumption 1, if 𝔼ξ​[F]{\mathbb{E}}_{\xi}[F] is LL-Lipschitz, then SEM (Alg.2) with a constant step size γ≤13​L\gamma\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}L} has the following convergence rate for any T≥1T\geq 1,

𝔼⁡[ErrR⁡(𝒚¯T)]≤R2γ​T+72​γ​σ2{\mathbb{E}}[\Err_{R}(\bar{\bm{y}}_{T})]\leq\frac{R^{2}}{\gamma T}+\frac{7}{2}\gamma\sigma^{2} (17)

where 𝐲¯T:=1T​∑t=0T−1𝐱t+1/2\bar{\bm{y}}_{T}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}{\bm{x}}_{t+1/2} and ErrR\Err_{R} is defined in (14). Particularly, γ=2​Rσ​7​T\gamma=\frac{\sqrt{2}R}{\sigma\sqrt{7T}} gives, 𝔼⁡[ErrR⁡(𝐲¯T)]≤14​R​σT{\mathbb{E}}[\Err_{R}(\bar{\bm{y}}_{T})]\leq\frac{\sqrt{14}R\sigma}{\sqrt{T}}.

As discussed previously, Assumption 2 is very strong in the unbounded setting, Thm. 2 does not require this assumption. Since in practice σ≪M\sigma\ll M, the variance term of SEM (17) is significantly smaller than the one of AvgSGD (16).

Re-using the minibatch for extragradient.

We now introduce a novel variant of the stochastic extragradient method (Alg. 3). The idea is to re-use the minibatch of the extrapolation step for the update of the current point. The intuition is that it correlates the estimator of the gradient of the extrapolation step and the one of the update step leading to a better correction of the oscillations which are also due to the stochasticity. One emerging issue (at least for the analysis) of this method is that since 𝒙t+12{\bm{x}}_{t+\frac{1}{2}} depend on ξt\xi_{t}, the quantity F⁡(𝒙t+12,ξt)F({\bm{x}}_{t+\frac{1}{2}},\xi_{t}) is a biased estimator of F⁡(𝒙t+12)F({\bm{x}}_{t+\frac{1}{2}}).

Theorem 3.

Let FF be a stochastic monotone operator, let 𝐱∗{\bm{x}}^{*} be a solution of (VIP) and let R>‖𝐱0−𝐱∗‖R>\|{\bm{x}}_{0}-{\bm{x}}^{*}\|. Let assume that ‖𝐲t−𝐱0‖≤R,∀t≥0\|{\bm{y}}_{t}-{\bm{x}}_{0}\|\leq R,\,\forall t\geq 0 where (𝐲t)({\bm{y}}_{t}) are the iterates of ReSEM. If the operator F⁡(⋅,ξ)F(\cdot,\xi) is LL-Lipschitz then under Assumption 1 for any T≥1,T\geq 1, ReSEM (Alg. 3) with constant step size γ≤12​L\gamma\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}L} has the following convergence:

𝔼⁡[ErrR⁡(𝒚¯T)]≤R2γ​T+γ​σ2+2​L2​(4​R2+σ2)2.{\mathbb{E}}[\Err_{R}(\bar{\bm{y}}_{T})]\leq\frac{R^{2}}{\gamma T}+\gamma\frac{\sigma^{2}+2L^{2}(4R^{2}+\sigma^{2})}{2}\,.

where 𝐲¯T:=1T​∑t=0T−1𝐱t+1/2\bar{\bm{y}}_{T}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}{\bm{x}}_{t+1/2} and ErrR\Err_{R} is defined in (14). Particularly, γt=γT\gamma_{t}=\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{T}} gives, 𝔼⁡[ErrR⁡(𝐲¯T)]≤O⁡(1)T{\mathbb{E}}[\Err_{R}(\bar{\bm{y}}_{T})]\leq\frac{O(1)}{\sqrt{T}}.

The assumption that the sequence of the iterates provided by the algorithm is bounded is stronger than for Theorem 2. Nevertheless, our preliminary experiment with a stochastic monotonone variational inequality yielded a reduced variance for ReSEM in comparison to SEM (see Fig. 2).

4.3 Comparison of the algorithms

To sum up, under Assumptions 1 and 2, and noticing that in practice σ≪M\sigma\ll M, the variance terms compare as follows:

SEM≤ReSEM≪AvgSGD≤PreSGD\text{SEM}\leq\text{ReSEM}\ll\text{AvgSGD}\leq\text{PreSGD} (18)

Both extragradient algorithms have significantly smaller variance than AvgSGD and PreSGD (Yadav et al., 2018).

5 Experiments

For our experiments, we consider the following algorithms:

  • •

    SimSGD: common SGD algorithm where both the parameters are updated simultaneously.

  • •

    AltSGD: variant of SGD where ϕ\phi is updated before θ\theta.

  • •

    AvgSGD: identical to simSGD, but we return the average of the iterates (see Alg. 1).

  • •

    SEM: stochastic extragradient method (see Alg. 2).

  • •

    ReSEM: re-used minibatch SEM (see Alg. 3).

5.1 Bilinear saddle point (stochastic)

We illustrate the performance of the various stochastic algorithms first on a simple (n=d=10n=d=10) finite sum bilinear objective (a monotone operator):

1n​∑i=1n(𝒙⊤​𝑴(i)​𝒚+𝒙⊤​𝒂(i)+𝒚⊤​𝒃(i)).\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left({\bm{x}}^{\top}\bm{M}^{(i)}{\bm{y}}+{\bm{x}}^{\top}\bm{a}^{(i)}+{\bm{y}}^{\top}\bm{b}^{(i)}\right). (19)

We generated randomly the coefficients of the matrices as well as the coefficients of the vectors 𝑴k​j(i),𝒂k(i),𝒃k(i)∼𝒩⁡(0,1), 1≤i≤n, 1≤j,k≤d\bm{M}^{(i)}_{kj},\,\bm{a}^{(i)}_{k},\,\bm{b}^{(i)}_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\,,\,1\leq i\leq n\,,\,1\leq j,k\leq d. The solution (𝒙∗,𝒚∗)({\bm{x}}^{*},{\bm{y}}^{*}) of this saddle point is simply the solution of the linear system

{𝑴¯​𝒚∗=−𝒂¯𝑴¯T​𝒙∗=−𝒃¯where𝑴¯=def1n∑i=1n𝑴(i),\left\{\begin{aligned} \bar{\bm{M}}{\bm{y}}^{*}&=-\bar{\bm{a}}\\ \bar{\bm{M}}^{T}{\bm{x}}^{*}&=-\bar{\bm{b}}\end{aligned}\right.\quad\text{where}\quad\bar{\bm{M}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{M}^{(i)},\, (20)

𝒂¯=def1n​∑i=1n𝒂(i)\bar{\bm{a}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{a}^{(i)} and 𝒃¯=def1n​∑i=1n𝒃(i).\bar{\bm{b}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{b}^{(i)}\,. The results are presented in Figure 2. We have tried the non averaged version of SEM and ReSEM, they have a similar noisy behavior as SimSGD. Moreover one can see that the ReSEM is more stable than the averaged SGD algorithm and performs the best on this task. As an averaging scheme, we used the weight ρt=t+1\rho_{t}=\sqrt{t+1} which is the weighted averaging scheme advised by Lacoste-Julien et al. (2012).

5.2 Toy non-convex GAN (2D and deterministic)

We now consider a task similar to (Mescheder, 2018) where the discriminator is linear Dϕ​(𝒙)=ϕT​𝒙D_{\phi}({\bm{x}})=\phi^{T}{\bm{x}}, the generator is a dirac distribution at θ\theta, qθ=δθq_{\theta}=\delta_{\theta} and the distribution we try to match is also a dirac at 𝒙0{\bm{x}}_{0}, p=δ𝒙0p=\delta_{{\bm{x}}_{0}}. The minimax formulation from Goodfellow et al. (2014) gives:

minθ⁡maxϕ−log⁡(1+e−ϕT​θ)−log⁡(1+eϕT​𝒙0)\min_{\theta}\max_{\phi}-\log\big(1+e^{-\phi^{T}\theta}\big)-\log\big(1+e^{\phi^{T}{\bm{x}}_{0}}\big) (21)

Note that as observed by Nagarajan and Kolter (2017), this objective is concave-concave, making it hard to optimize. We compare the methods on this objective where we take 𝒙0=−2{\bm{x}}_{0}=-2, thus the position of the equilibrium is shifted towards the position (−2,0)(-2,0). The convergence and the gradient vector field are shown in Figure 3. We observe that only SEM converges fast, however note that if we were to let all methods run for a long time they would all end up converging, although the convergence would be really slow.

5.3 WGAN on CIFAR10

We now consider a more challenging task (non-convex and stochastic) with a standard GAN benchmark. We train the DCGAN architecture from Radford et al. (2016) with the WGAN objective from Arjovsky et al. (2017), on the CIFAR10 dataset (Krizhevsky and Hinton, 2009). We compare all the methods using the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2015) with learning rate γ=0.0001\gamma=0.0001 and β1=0.5\beta_{1}=0.5 (see details in Appendix C). Note that here AltSGD refers to a version where we update the parameters of the discriminator 5 times before updating the parameters of the generator, as done in the original WGAN paper (updating the discriminator only once yields results similar to SimSGD). For all methods, we compare a non-averaged version with a uniformly averaged version (denoted by the prefix Avg in front of the name of the method). We train all the methods with 5 different random seeds for 200,000 iterations of the generator, reporting the inception score (Salimans et al., 2016) at every 1000 iterations on 1000 example. The results are shown in Fig. 4. We can observe that both SEM and ReSEM perform better in terms of inception score, and using averaging enables to achieve even higher inception score.

We also compared all the methods in the same setting, but using the WGAN-GP objective from Gulrajani et al. (2017). For all methods we plot the results obtained with the best learning rate in Fig. 4. We can see that SEM works almost as well as AltSGD which updates the discriminator 5 more times before updating the generator. Note that SEM is faster to run since it only requires to do two forward pass instead of six. Also, for SEM, the gradient for the generator and discriminator can be computed easily in parallel, thus in practice we observe that SEM is almost 2 times faster. We also observe that both variants of SEM are more stable which enables us to use bigger learning rate, up to γ=10−3\gamma=10^{-3} whereas the other methods do not perform as well at higher learning rates. Further results and samples are presented in Appendix C.

6 Related Work

Now that we have introduced a more general framework optimizing in GANs, we can look at the previous work thought the prism of the variational inequality literature. The extragradient method is the standard algorithm to optimize variational inequalities. This algorithm has been originally introduced by Korpelevich (1976) and extended by Nesterov (2007) and Nemirovski (2004). Stochastic versions of the extragradient have been recently analyzed (Juditsky et al., 2011; Yousefian et al., 2014; Iusem et al., 2017) in the context of stochastic variational inequalities with bounded constraints. A linearly convergent variance reduced version of the stochastic gradient method has been proposed by Palaniappan and Bach (2016) for strongly monotone variational inequalities.

A first idea to optimize the two-players game (3) is to sequentially fully optimize the discriminator for a fixed generator, then make a gradient step for this “optimal” discriminator, and repeat this process. This way of optimizing (3) can be related with (Arjovsky et al., 2017) where several updates (ncritic=5n_{\text{critic}}=5 in practice) are processed on the discriminator between each update of the generator. It is also the case in (Metz et al., 2017) where they explicitly try to construct the “true generator objective function” unrolling for KK steps. Nevertheless the fact that this “true generator function” cannot be found with a satisfying accuracy may lead to a different behavior that the one expected.

Several methods to stabilize GANs consist in transforming the minimax formulation (SP) into a more general variational inequality that can no longer be cast as a saddle point problem. This is the case of the non-saturating formulation of GANs (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Fedus et al., 2017), the DCGANs (Radford et al., 2016), the gradient penalty55 5 (Gulrajani et al., 2017, Eq.(3)) is a bit confusing but one can notice that in their Alg. 1 the gradient penalty is only added to the discriminator cost function. Since this gradient penalty depends also on the generator, WGAN-GP cannot be cast as a SP problem. for WGANs (Gulrajani et al., 2017). Yadav et al. (2018) propose an optimization method for GANs based on AltSGD using a momentum based extrapolation step on the generator. Mescheder et al. (2017) propose to add the norm of the gradient in the objective and provide an interesting perspective on GANs, interpreting the training as the research of a two-players game equilibrium. A study of the continuous version of two player games has been done by Ratliff et al. (2016) and interesting non-convex results have been proved in the context of GANs by Grnarova et al. (2018).

7 Conclusion

We have presented a new framework called variational inequality to consider GAN objectives. We tapped into the optimization literature to bring new techniques to train GANs and provided empirical as well as theoretical evidence on the benefits of averaging and extrapolation steps. On one hand, the former seems to improve the inception score at convergence, on the other hand the latter looks to be more stable for step size tuning. Nevertheless, we just considered two standard algorithms. We have just scratched the surface and hope it opens the door to a new algorithmic perspective on training GANs.

Appendix A Definitions

In this section we recall usual definition and lemmas from convex analysis. we start with a simple definition.

Definition 1.

The projection P𝒳P_{\mathcal{X}} onto 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} is defined as,

P𝒳​(𝒚)=def𝐚𝐫𝐠​𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐱∈𝒳⁡‖𝐱−𝐲‖22.P_{\mathcal{X}}({\bm{y}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\argmin_{{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}}\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|_{2}^{2}\,. (22)

We recall a property we used in all our proofs, the non-expansiveness of the projection onto a convex set.

Lemma 1.

Let 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} a convex set, the projection mapping P𝒳:ℝd→𝒳P_{\mathcal{X}}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathcal{X}} is nonexpansive, i.e.,

‖P𝒳​(𝒙)−P𝒳​(𝒙′)‖2≤‖𝒙−𝒙′‖2,∀𝒙,𝒙′∈𝒳.\|P_{\mathcal{X}}({\bm{x}})-P_{\mathcal{X}}({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\|_{2}\,,\quad\forall{\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{X}}\,. (23)

This is standard convex analysis result which can be found for instance in [Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004].

Another important property used in our proof is the Lipschitzness of an operator.

Definition 2.

A mapping F:ℝp→ℝdF\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is said to be LL-Lipschitz if,

‖F⁡(𝒙)−F⁡(𝒙′)‖2≤L​‖𝒙−𝒙′‖2,∀𝒙,𝒙′∈𝒳.\|F({\bm{x}})-F({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq L\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\|_{2}\,,\quad\forall{\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{X}}\,. (24)
Definition 3.

A differentiable function f:𝒳→ℝf\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}{\mathcal{X}}\to{\mathbb{R}} is said to be μ\mu-strongly convex if

f(𝒙)≥f(𝒚)+∇f(𝒚)⊤(𝒙−𝒚)+μ2∥𝒙−𝒚∥22∀𝒙,𝒚∈𝒳.f({\bm{x}})\geq f({\bm{y}})+\nabla f({\bm{y}})^{\top}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}})+\frac{\mu}{2}\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|_{2}^{2}\,\quad\forall{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{X}}\,. (25)
Definition 4.

A function (θ,ϕ)↦ℒ⁡(θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi)\mapsto{\mathcal{L}}(\theta,\phi) is said convex-concave if ℒ⁡(⋅,ϕ){\mathcal{L}}(\cdot,\phi) is convex for all ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi and ℒ⁡(θ,⋅){\mathcal{L}}(\theta,\cdot) is concave for all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta. An ℒ{\mathcal{L}} is said to be μ\mu-strongly convex concave if (θ,ϕ)↦ℒ⁡(θ,ϕ)−μ2​‖θ‖22+μ2​‖ϕ‖22(\theta,\phi)\mapsto{\mathcal{L}}(\theta,\phi)-\frac{\mu}{2}\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\mu}{2}\|\phi\|_{2}^{2} is convex concave.

Definition 5.

An operator F:𝒳→ℝdF\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}{\mathcal{X}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is said to be μ\mu-strongly monotone if

(F⁡(𝒙)−F⁡(𝒚))⊤​(𝒙−𝒚)≥μ​‖𝒙−𝒚‖22.(F({\bm{x}})-F({\bm{y}}))^{\top}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}})\geq\mu\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|^{2}_{2}\,. (26)

Appendix B Proof of Theorems

This section is dedicated on the proof of the theorems provided in this paper,

Proof.

Let any 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} such that ‖𝒙0−𝒙‖≤R\|{\bm{x}}_{0}-{\bm{x}}\|\leq R,

‖𝒙t+1−𝒙‖22\displaystyle\|{\bm{x}}_{t+1}-{\bm{x}}\|^{2}_{2} =‖P𝒳​(𝒙t−γt​F​(𝒙t,ξt))−𝒙‖22\displaystyle=\|P_{\mathcal{X}}({\bm{x}}_{t}-\gamma_{t}F({\bm{x}}_{t},\xi_{t}))-{\bm{x}}\|_{2}^{2}
≤∥𝒙t−γtF(𝒙t,ξt))−𝒙∥22\displaystyle\leq\|{\bm{x}}_{t}-\gamma_{t}F({\bm{x}}_{t},\xi_{t}))-{\bm{x}}\|_{2}^{2}
(projections are non-contractive, Lemma 1)\displaystyle\quad(\text{projections are non-contractive, Lemma\penalty\ \ref{lem:proj_non_contr}})
=‖𝒙t−𝒙‖22−2​γt​F​(𝒙t,ξt)⊤​(𝒙t−𝒙)+‖γt​F​(𝒙t,ξt)‖22\displaystyle=\|{\bm{x}}_{t}-{\bm{x}}\|^{2}_{2}-2\gamma_{t}F({\bm{x}}_{t},\xi_{t})^{\top}({\bm{x}}_{t}-{\bm{x}})+\|\gamma_{t}F({\bm{x}}_{t},\xi_{t})\|^{2}_{2}

Then we can make appear the quantity F​(𝒙t)⊤​(𝒙t−𝒙)F({\bm{x}}_{t})^{\top}({\bm{x}}_{t}-{\bm{x}}) on the LHS,

we can sum (27) for 0≤t≤T−10\leq t\leq T-1 to get,

2​∑t=0T−1γt​F​(𝒙t)⊤​(𝒙t−𝒙)≤∑t=0T−1[(‖𝒙t−𝒙‖2−‖𝒙t+1−𝒙‖2)+γt2​‖F⁡(𝒙t,ξt)‖22+2​γt​Δt⊤​(𝒙t−𝒙)]2\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma_{t}F({\bm{x}}_{t})^{\top}({\bm{x}}_{t}-{\bm{x}})\leq\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\left[(\|{\bm{x}}_{t}-{\bm{x}}\|^{2}-\|{\bm{x}}_{t+1}-{\bm{x}}\|^{2})+\gamma^{2}_{t}\|F({\bm{x}}_{t},\xi_{t})\|^{2}_{2}+2\gamma_{t}\Delta_{t}^{\top}({\bm{x}}_{t}-{\bm{x}})\right] (28)

B.2 Proof of Thm.2

In order to prove Thm.2 we will prove a lemma

Lemma 3.

Let 𝐱∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} and 𝐱+=defP𝒳​(𝐱+𝐮){\bm{x}}^{+}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}P_{\mathcal{X}}({\bm{x}}+{\bm{u}}) then for all 𝐲∈𝒳{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{X}} we have,

‖𝒙+−𝒚‖22≤‖𝒙−𝒚‖22+2​𝒖⊤​(𝒙+−𝒚)−‖𝒙+−𝒙‖22.\|{\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{y}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|_{2}^{2}+2{\bm{u}}^{\top}({\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{y}})-\|{\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{x}}\|_{2}^{2}\,. (41)
Proof of Lemma 3.

We start y simply developing,

‖𝒙+−𝒚‖22=‖(𝒙+−𝒙)+(𝒙−𝒚)‖22\displaystyle\|{\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{y}}\|_{2}^{2}=\|({\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{x}})+({\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}})\|_{2}^{2} =‖𝒙−𝒚‖22+2​(𝒙+−𝒙)⊤​(𝒙−𝒚)+‖𝒙+−𝒙‖22\displaystyle=\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|_{2}^{2}+2({\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{x}})^{\top}({\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}})+\|{\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{x}}\|_{2}^{2}
=‖𝒙−𝒚‖22+2​(𝒙+−𝒙)⊤​(𝒙+−𝒚)−‖𝒙+−𝒙‖22.\displaystyle=\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|_{2}^{2}+2({\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{x}})^{\top}({\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{y}})-\|{\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{x}}\|_{2}^{2}\,.

Then since 𝒙+{\bm{x}}^{+} is the projection onto the convex set 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} of 𝒙+𝒖{\bm{x}}+{\bm{u}} we have that (𝒙+−(𝒙+𝒖))⊤​(𝒙+−𝒚)≤0,∀𝒚∈𝒳({\bm{x}}^{+}-({\bm{x}}+{\bm{u}}))^{\top}({\bm{x}}^{+}-{\bm{y}})\leq 0\,,\;\forall\,{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{X}}, leading to the result of the Lemma. ∎

We can then proof Thm.2.

leading to

Appendix C Additional experimental results

Adam.

For all the methods and experiments on CIFAR10, we used the Adam optimizer. We want to emphasize that we use Adam as it is commonly used in the literature to get state of the art results in practice. However, our theoretical analysis does not cover it. While it is straightforward to use Adam with SimSGD and AltSGD, it requires a little bit more discussion for SEM. In the paper, we consider the operator FF to be defined as:

F⁡(𝒙)=(∇θℒ(θ)​(θ,ϕ)∇ϕℒ(ϕ)​(θ,ϕ)),F({\bm{x}})=\begin{pmatrix}\nabla_{\theta}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\theta)}(\theta,\phi)\\ \nabla_{\phi}{\mathcal{L}}^{(\phi)}(\theta,\phi)\end{pmatrix}\,, (47)

When using Adam, we replace the gradient in (47) by the update from Adam:

FA​d​a​m​(𝒙)=(m^θv^θ+ϵm^ϕv^ϕ+ϵ),F_{Adam}({\bm{x}})=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\hat{m}_{\theta}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_{\theta}+\epsilon}}\\ \frac{\hat{m}_{\phi}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_{\phi}+\epsilon}}\end{pmatrix}\,, (48)

where m^θ\hat{m}_{\theta}, m^ϕ\hat{m}_{\phi} , v^θ\hat{v}_{\theta} and v^ϕ\hat{v}_{\phi} are the first and second bias-corrected momentum computed by Adam. When using Adam with SEM, we then simply replace F⁡(𝒙)F({\bm{x}}) in Alg. 2 by FA​d​a​m​(𝒙)F_{Adam}({\bm{x}}).
